title: Judging number predictions
subtitle: Two spend models, two error measures, two different winners. Which one do you believe?
goal: After this lesson you can choose the error measure for a predicted number (MAE, RMSE or total error) from what a miss costs, and explain why two measures can rank the same models differently.

predict.q: Two made-up spend models, 100 advertisers. Model 1 is off by $1,000 on every one of them. Model 2 is exactly right on 99 and off by $100,000 on the last. Which has the larger average miss?
options: Model 1
Model 2
Neither: the two are equal
It cannot be worked out from this
predict.reveal: Neither: both miss by $1,000 on average. The lesson shows the measure that tells them apart, and when it should decide between two real models.

segments.narration: Finance wants a number for every advertiser: how much will they spend over the next eight weeks. You ask your assistant for two candidate models. Call them model A and model B. How they work inside comes later. The assistant's note says B has the lower error, so ship B. You ask for a second error measure, on the same test advertisers, and now A is ahead. Neither number is wrong. Until now the prediction was a yes or a no. For a number, there are several honest ways to score a miss, and they do not always agree. The same holds for any model that predicts a number, such as the CPA a new campaign will reach.

visual.title: Judging number predictions
visual.sub: When each model wins on a different measure

segments.narration: Start with one advertiser. The model predicted one amount, they spent another, and the gap between the two is the miss. [[1]] Do that for every test advertiser, ignore whether each miss was high or low, and average. That is the mean absolute error, MAE: the average miss, in dollars. [[2]] As always, it needs a bar to beat. The laziest forecast says each advertiser will spend what they spent in the last eight weeks. It misses by about 2,400 dollars. [[3]] A sharper one doubles the most recent four weeks. Call it the run-rate. It misses by about 2,000 dollars, and that is the bar.

visual.title: MAE: the average miss, in dollars

segments.narration: Both candidates clear the bar. [[3]] [[4]] Model A and model B each miss by about 1,700 dollars on average, and B is ahead by 58 dollars. Before you believe that, ask how much of that gap is luck. Score the same two models on a different draw of advertisers and the gap moves. Here it could plausibly sit anywhere from about 180 dollars in B's favour to about 70 in A's. That range crosses zero. On average miss, then, this is a tie. More on that check in the next lesson.

visual.title: Average miss (MAE), 4,000 test advertisers
visual.note: B minus A: −$58, plausible range −$177 to +$73. A tie. Inside the models: A in lesson 3-1, B in lesson 4-3.

segments.narration: Now a second way to keep score. Picture two made-up models and 100 advertisers. [[1]] The first is off by 1,000 dollars on every single one. [[2]] The second is exactly right on 99 of them and off by 100,000 dollars on the last. Same MAE: 1,000 dollars each. Would finance call them equally good? The second measure says no. Square every miss, average the squares, then take the square root to get back to dollars. That is root mean squared error, RMSE. Squaring means a miss ten times bigger counts a hundred times more. The steady model scores 1,000. The model with one disaster scores 10,000.

visual.title: Toy example: 100 advertisers, same MAE
visual.note: RMSE: square each miss, average, take the square root.

segments.narration: Back to the real candidates. [[1]] Model A has an RMSE of about 4,900 dollars. [[2]] Model B, about 5,800. Same average miss, but when B is badly wrong, it is wrong by more. So which model wins depends on what a miss costs. If one huge surprise on a big account hurts more than a hundred small errors, judge by RMSE and take A. If every dollar of error costs the same, judge by MAE, call it a tie, and take whichever is simpler to run. Make that choice before you see the scoreboard, not after. That ordering comes from one simulated test set, and RMSE leans on a few accounts. On your data it may flip.

visual.title: Same average miss, different big misses

segments.narration: Finance will also add your predictions up into a revenue number. MAE and RMSE both ignore direction, so neither says whether that sum comes out right. R-squared, which assistants like to print, does not either: it is the share of the variation explained, a fraction, not dollars. For that, compare the predicted total with the actual total. [[1]] The same-as-last forecast comes out about 23 percent low. [[2]] The run-rate, about 20 percent low. In this simulated world total spend grows from one period to the next, and a forecast that repeats the past cannot see growth. [[3]] [[4]] Models A and B both come out about 6 percent high. Misses that lean one way are called bias, and bias does not average out. It adds up.

One more habit. An average miss describes nobody in particular. Leave A and B for a moment and take the stronger spend model you will meet in module five. Cut its test advertisers into thirds by past spend. [[1]] On small accounts it misses by about 170 dollars. [[2]] [[3]] On large accounts, by over 3,300. A small group of advertisers carries nearly half of all its error, and the worst single miss was a large account forecast at about 133,000 dollars that left and spent nothing. So ask for error by size tier, and for the biggest misses by name.

visual.title: One overall MAE of $1,416, three different stories
visual.note: A stronger spend model, from lesson 5-5. 46% of its total error comes from 5% of advertisers.

segments.narration: So, the brief. Ask your assistant to predict spend for the next eight weeks and to score it on the test advertisers only. The output must show four things. [[1]] Both baselines beside every model, on the same rows. [[2]] Three measures side by side: MAE, RMSE, and predicted total against actual total. [[3]] Error by size tier, with the ten largest misses listed. [[4]] And one trap. If it quotes an average percentage error, ask what happened to the zeros. About one test advertiser in eight spent nothing, and you cannot divide by zero. Those rows were dropped or patched, and the output has to say which. [[5]] Need a percentage? Ask for total absolute error divided by total actual spend, which a zero cannot break.

visual.title: Brief and audit: what the output must show
items: Both baselines beside every model, same test rows
MAE, RMSE and predicted total vs actual total
Error by size tier, plus the ten largest misses
Zero-spend rows (13.2% here): how did a percentage error treat them?
Need a percentage? Total absolute error ÷ total actual spend

segments.narration: The next time someone asks which forecast is better, answer with a question: what does a big miss cost you, and what does a small one? One thread is still loose, that 58 dollar gap that might be luck, and telling real from noise is the next lesson.

visual.text: Pick the error measure from what a miss costs. Then look at the scoreboard.
visual.sub: MAE: every dollar counts the same · RMSE: big misses count most · Total: do the misses cancel?

takeaways: MAE is the average miss in dollars; RMSE makes large misses count far more.
The two can rank models differently, so choose the measure from what a miss costs before you compare.
Then look past the average: the total, the size tiers, the largest misses and the zeros.

quiz.q: Two spend models are scored on the same 4,000 test advertisers. Model A: MAE $1,733, RMSE $4,878. Model B: MAE $1,675, RMSE $5,824. Finance says one large surprise on a big account costs them far more than many small misses. Which model do you put forward?
options: B: its MAE is lower, and MAE is the measure that is stated in dollars
A: RMSE weights large misses most, and those are what finance fears
Either: a $58 gap in MAE is a tie, and a tie on MAE makes the two models interchangeable
B: a lower MAE means its RMSE will also come out lower on new data
quiz.why: Finance has said a large miss costs disproportionately more, which is what RMSE measures, and A's RMSE is lower ($4,878 against $5,824). B's $58 edge on MAE is tiny, but a tie on one measure does not make two models interchangeable when their large misses differ. Both measures are in dollars, so 'MAE is the dollar one' is not a reason to prefer it.

quiz.q: The assistant writes: 'Baseline: same as last 8 weeks, MAE $2,404 per advertiser. Good enough for a first revenue plan, so I summed the predictions for finance.' The output hides a flaw. What do you check before finance uses that sum?
options: The RMSE: if it is lower than the MAE, the large misses are under control and the sum is safe
The row count: across 4,000 advertisers the misses cancel, so the sum only needs enough rows
The MAE as a share of average spend: if it is under half, the summed plan is within tolerance
The direction of the misses: predicted total against actual total, which runs about 23% low here
quiz.why: MAE averages the size of the misses and throws away their direction, so it cannot say whether a sum is right. This baseline's misses lean low, and the summed plan undershoots actual spend by about 23%. More rows do not cancel misses that lean one way, and RMSE is never lower than MAE, so that check cannot pass.

quiz.q: Lead scoring. A model predicts each new lead's first-month revenue. About 30% of leads never buy, so their actual revenue is zero. The assistant reports: 'Average percentage error: 22%.' What is the right read?
options: It can only describe the leads that bought: ask for the dollar error on all leads
It is sound as long as it beats the baseline's percentage error
The model gets about 22% of the leads wrong, which is better than the 30% who never buy
It should be converted to RMSE, which handles zero-revenue leads correctly, before anyone judges it
quiz.why: A percentage error divides by the actual value, and you cannot divide by zero, so the leads that never bought were dropped or patched before that 22% was computed. Beating a baseline on the same crippled measure does not repair it, 22% is the size of a miss, not the share of leads the model got wrong, and converting to RMSE does not bring the dropped leads back.

quiz.concept: averages hide where the error falls
quiz.q: A spend model's overall MAE is $1,416. An account manager whose book is all small accounts, averaging about $500 of spend, says: 'Off by $1,400 on a $500 account? Useless to me.' What do you tell her?
options: She is right: an error nearly three times the size of the account makes the model unusable for her book
She should judge it by RMSE instead, because RMSE is the fairer measure for small accounts
The overall figure is driven by large accounts: look at the miss in her own size tier, about $170
The model misses every account by about $1,416, so it only suits books of large accounts
quiz.why: An overall MAE mixes tiers: for this model the miss is about $170 on small accounts and over $3,300 on large ones, and nearly half of all error comes from 5% of advertisers. Applying the overall average to one small account is the mistake, and RMSE would be dominated by large accounts even more.

review.concept: MAE or RMSE: choose by what a miss costs

variants.q: Two daily revenue forecasts for the treasury team. Forecast X: MAE $9,000, RMSE $11,000. Forecast Y: MAE $8,000, RMSE $25,000. A day that is badly off forces an expensive overnight loan; small daily errors cost almost nothing. Which forecast suits them?
options: Y, because its average miss is $1,000 smaller on an ordinary day
X, because its much lower RMSE shows it avoids the badly wrong days
Y, because RMSE is larger than MAE for every forecast, so the gap between them means little
Neither yet: first find out what share of days each forecast got exactly right
variants.why: The cost here comes from rare large misses, and RMSE is the measure that weights them: Y's RMSE is more than twice X's, so Y has days that are far off. Y's slightly lower MAE only says its ordinary days are a little closer, which is not what treasury pays for.

variants.q: A model predicts how many minutes each support ticket will take, to estimate each agent's daily workload. Every minute of error matters equally. Model P: MAE 6 minutes, RMSE 9. Model Q: MAE 4.5 minutes, RMSE 14. Which do you choose?
options: P, because a lower RMSE is the safer choice whatever the errors cost
Q, because its average miss is lower; note its few large misses
P, because Q's RMSE is about three times its MAE, the sign of a broken model
Q, because a higher RMSE shows that it captures more of the variation in tickets
variants.why: When each minute of error costs the same, the average miss is the cost, so the lower MAE wins. Q's high RMSE tells you a few tickets are badly misjudged, which is worth knowing, but 'lower RMSE is always safer' ignores what a miss costs in this use.

variants.q: The assistant compares two models that predict next-8-week spend and reports one line: 'Both have an MAE of about $1,700, so they are equivalent.' Which follow-up tests that claim best?
options: Ask for the accuracy of each model at a sensible cut-off
Ask for the MAE again, this time on the training rows
Ask for the MAE to more decimal places, to break the tie
Ask for the RMSE of each, and for each model's ten largest misses
variants.why: Equal average misses can hide very different large misses; RMSE and a list of the biggest misses expose them. Accuracy does not apply to a predicted number, error on the training rows says nothing about new advertisers, and more decimals of the same average still hide the large misses.

review.concept: Bias: small misses that lean one way add up in a total

variants.q: An upsell model predicts the extra monthly spend of each account after an upgrade. The per-account MAE is small, $40. Finance sums the predictions and the total is 18% above what actually came in. What explains both facts?
options: The misses lean one way: most predictions are a little high, and across every account that adds up
The MAE must have been computed on the training rows, where every model looks better
Misses of $40 are too small to move a total, so the sum itself was computed wrongly
An 18% gap in the total is what a $40 MAE normally produces once it is summed
variants.why: MAE ignores direction, so small misses that all lean high look harmless per account and still pile up in a sum. Small per-account errors only protect a total when they point both ways and cancel.

variants.q: A model predicts how many days each creative will last before its CTR fades. Its average miss is 2 days. The refresh calendar built from it keeps replacing creatives after they have already faded. What should you ask the assistant for?
options: The RMSE, to see whether a few creatives have very large misses
A larger training set of creatives, since 2 days is already a small miss
The average signed miss: are predictions mostly too long?
The same MAE broken down by vertical, to find where it is worst
variants.why: Refreshes that are consistently late point to predictions that lean one way, and MAE cannot show direction; the average of predicted minus actual can. RMSE would reveal a few large misses, not a consistent tilt.

variants.q: Per-advertiser spend predictions have an MAE of $300 across 5,000 advertisers. The CFO asks: 'So the total will be off by about $1.5 million?' What is the accurate answer?
options: Yes: the error of the total is the MAE times the number of advertisers
No: with 5,000 advertisers the misses always cancel, so the total is nearly exact
No: the error of the total is the RMSE times the number of advertisers
It depends on direction: compare the predicted total with the actual total
variants.why: MAE counts every miss as positive, so $1.5 million is the sum of the miss sizes, not the error of the sum. If the misses lean one way the total can be off by nearly that much; if they balance it can be almost exact. Only predicted total against actual total tells you.

drill.q: Two models have the same average miss, but one has a much higher root mean squared error. What does that tell you about it?
drill.a: It makes a few very large misses. Squaring makes big misses count far more, so its root mean squared error climbs while its average miss stays the same.

drill.q: Per-customer predictions are going to be added up into a revenue forecast. Besides the average miss, which number do you ask for, and why?
drill.a: Predicted total against actual total. The average miss ignores direction, so misses that all lean low can look small for each customer and still leave the total far short.

recall.prompt: A colleague says: 'Model B has the lower MAE, so B is the better spend model.' In 30 seconds, what else would you want to know before agreeing?
recall.model_answer: MAE is the average miss and treats every dollar of error alike, so first ask what a miss costs: if rare huge misses hurt most, compare RMSE, where the order can reverse. Then check whether the gap is bigger than chance, whether the predicted total matches the actual total, and where the error sits: by size tier and in the largest misses. Any percentage error needs a second look wherever the actual is zero.

ask_assistant: Predict [the number] for each [unit], training on [training period] and scoring only on [test rows the model never saw]. In one table, on the same rows, show [the simplest baseline, such as same as last period], [a sharper baseline if there is one] and each model, with MAE, RMSE and predicted total versus actual total, and state the row count. Add MAE by [size tier or segment] and list the [10] largest misses with predicted and actual values. State how many test rows have an actual value of zero and how many rows any percentage error was computed on; if I need a percentage, use total absolute error divided by total actual.
audit_checklist: Both baselines and every model scored on the same test rows, with the row count stated
MAE, RMSE and predicted total versus actual total side by side
Error by size tier and a list of the largest individual misses
The count of rows with zero actual spend, and the row count behind any percentage error: if it is smaller than the test set, rows were dropped
transfer: Forecasting daily platform spend for finance: is one badly wrong day worse than many slightly wrong days?
Predicting how long support tickets take, to plan staffing: does each ticket matter, or the day's total?
Estimating the CPA a new campaign will reach before an account manager promises it to a client: what does a large miss cost?

other_ways.when: When you want the miss for the advertiser in the middle and a few giant accounts should not move the number.

other_ways.approach: Total absolute error divided by total actual spend
other_ways.when: When stakeholders want a percentage: it weights by dollars and does not break on advertisers who spent zero.

other_ways.approach: Share of predictions within a stated tolerance
other_ways.when: When the business has a clear 'close enough', such as within $200, and wants a hit rate it can track.

glossary.def: Mean absolute error: the average size of a miss, ignoring direction, in the units of the prediction.
Root mean squared error: square the misses, average them, take the square root; large misses count far more.
Misses that lean one way on average, so the predicted total lands above or below the actual total.
Predicted total divided by actual total, minus one: the measure that matters when predictions are summed.
A baseline that doubles the most recent four weeks of spend to predict the next eight.

The share of the variation in actual values that the predictions explain: 1 is perfect, 0 is no better than the average. Built from squared misses, it ranks models like RMSE, but it is a fraction, not dollars.
